account: Bedi, Al Masri, Al Hennawi, Qadir and Ottman are internal medicine physicians at Abington Jefferson Hospital in Abington, United States, with a co-author at Alfaisal University in Riyadh. On 9 March 2023 they reported in Cureus the case of a 25-year-old man with anxiety and depression. The report gives no date for the event. The man came to an emergency department with 24 hours of chest pressure and palpitations. His smartwatch had notified him several times of an irregular rhythm consistent with atrial fibrillation. The authors link the arrhythmia to weekend binge drinking. His heart rate was above 120 beats per minute (bpm). The electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response at 123 bpm. Intravenous diltiazem and oral metoprolol did not restore the rhythm. Enoxaparin was started. His B-type natriuretic peptide level was 796, and a chest X-ray was clear. He was admitted. On the cardiologist's recommendation, he underwent electrical cardioversion guided by transesophageal echocardiography the next day, which restored sinus rhythm. Despite a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0, he was given apixaban for four weeks. He was advised to stop drinking alcohol and to return gradually to exercise. Monthly cardiology follow-up was scheduled. The report names neither the brand nor the model of the watch. It describes smartwatches generically as using photoplethysmography with deep neural network algorithms.
